prompt: What is the main point of the text?
passage:
Anyone who has tried to hold a conversation beside a busy road knows the instinctive remedy: you raise your voice, and perhaps its pitch, until you are heard. Birds, it turns out, do something similar. In many cities, songbirds of several species sing at a higher pitch than their relatives in the quieter countryside, apparently lifting their songs clear of the low rumble of traffic. Some sing more loudly; some start earlier, before the morning rush begins; a few have taken to singing at night, when the streets are quieter.

It is tempting to read such findings as evolution caught in the act, and headlines have rarely resisted the temptation. Cities are young, the argument runs, so any trait that sets urban populations apart must have arisen at remarkable speed. The story appeals because it turns the city, usually cast as nature's enemy, into a laboratory in which natural selection can be watched at work.

The trouble is that a difference between two populations says nothing, on its own, about how the difference came about. A bird that sings higher in a city may carry genes that its rural cousins lack, but it may equally be an ordinary bird doing what birds of its kind have always been able to do: adjusting its song to its surroundings, much as we adjust our voices in a crowded restaurant. Individual birds of some species have been observed raising and lowering their pitch as the noise around them rises and falls, which is hard to square with the idea of a fixed, inherited trait. Telling the two explanations apart requires patient work—raising birds from different populations under identical conditions, for instance—and such studies are slow, expensive and, by the standards of a news cycle, unexciting.

None of this makes urban song less interesting. If anything, the case for flexibility raises a sharper question. Many species have never settled in cities at all, while others have moved in with apparent ease. Perhaps what distinguishes the successful newcomers is not a change acquired after arrival but a capacity they brought with them: a readiness to vary their behaviour when circumstances change. On this view, the city does not so much create new kinds of birds as sort existing ones, admitting those that were adaptable to begin with and quietly turning the rest away.

That is a less dramatic story than evolution at high speed, but it may prove the more useful one. If flexibility is the price of admission, then the species we should worry about as cities spread are not those that already share our streets, but those whose habits are too fixed to follow.
options: Traffic noise has forced urban songbirds to evolve higher-pitched songs in a remarkably short time.
Only slow and patient research can show whether city birds really sing differently from rural ones.
The way city birds sing may say more about adaptability than about rapid genetic change.
City birds may have evolved their flexible way of singing as a response to urban noise.
explain: The author grants that urban birds sing differently but argues that the difference 'says nothing, on its own' about its cause, that it may equally reflect birds adjusting their song, and that such adaptability may also explain which species manage to settle in cities at all, so the songs may say more about adaptability than about rapid genetic change. The idea that traffic noise has forced rapid evolution is the headline reading the author questions. The suggestion that birds evolved their flexibility in response to city noise contradicts the text, which presents flexibility as 'a capacity they brought with them', not 'a change acquired after arrival'. Patient research is said to be needed to tell the two explanations apart, not to establish whether city birds sing differently, which the text treats as an observed fact.

prompt: Why, according to the author, can closer inspection not solve the main problem?
passage:
Every organisation that tries to manage by numbers sooner or later runs into the same awkward fact. A figure that once told you something useful about how well people were working starts, the moment you reward or punish them according to it, to tell you mainly how good they have become at producing that figure. Economists call this Goodhart's law, after the British economist who described it, but few of us need the name. We have all heard of call centres that time their calls and end up with staff who cut difficult customers off, or of schools judged on exam results that quietly stop entering pupils who might fail.

The usual response is outrage, followed by tighter rules. On this account the trouble is cheating: a few unscrupulous individuals game the system, and the cure is closer inspection. Cheating certainly happens, but it is not the heart of the problem. Far more common, and far harder to detect, is the conscientious employee who simply does what she has been asked. Told that her performance will be judged on a single number, she devotes her limited time and attention to that number, and the parts of her job that nobody counts—the patient explanation, the colleague helped out of a tight spot—shrink without anyone ever deciding that they should. No rule has been broken. That is precisely why inspection cannot fix it.

It does not follow that we should throw our measurements away. Organisations that abandon numbers altogether tend to fall back on impressions, and impressions are hardly free of bias; they favour the confident, the visible and the familiar. A hospital that stops recording waiting times does not thereby become kinder to its patients. The question is not whether to measure but what to do with the measurements once we have them.

Here a distinction that is often blurred in practice becomes useful. A number can serve as the start of a conversation or as a verdict. In the first case, a sudden drop in a team's figures prompts someone to go and find out what is happening, and the answer may well be that the team is doing something valuable that the number cannot see. In the second, the same drop sets off an automatic penalty, and the team learns to protect the number rather than explain it. The figures are identical in both cases; what differs is whether anyone is still expected to exercise judgement.

Such judgement does not come cheap. It requires managers who understand the work well enough to see what the numbers leave out, and it cannot be scaled up as easily as a spreadsheet. But the alternative is not objectivity. It is an organisation that knows more and more about less and less.
options: Because conscientious employees hide from inspectors the parts of the job they neglect
Because the problem lies in what people are asked to do, not in people breaking rules
Because inspectors tend to favour the confident, the visible and the familiar
Because cheating has become far too widespread to be investigated properly
explain: The author argues that the main problem is not cheating but the conscientious employee who 'simply does what she has been asked', concentrating on the number she is judged by while the uncounted parts of the job shrink; no rule is broken, which is 'precisely why inspection cannot fix it'. This behaviour is 'far harder to detect' because nothing is being broken, not because employees hide what they neglect; the text says the shrinking happens 'without anyone ever deciding that they should'. The bias towards the confident, the visible and the familiar is attributed to impressions, not to inspectors. And the claim that cheating is too widespread contradicts the statement that cheating 'is not the heart of the problem'.

prompt: What is the main point of the text?
passage: In a famous passage of his Confessions, Augustine describes watching Ambrose, the bishop of Milan, at his reading: his eyes ran over the page and his heart searched out the meaning, but his voice and tongue were still. For generations the scene was cited as proof that silent reading was a rarity in the ancient world—an oddity worth writing down. The inference is weaker than it looks. Ambrose was not alone in a study when Augustine saw him; he read in this way while visitors sat waiting to speak with him. And Augustine's own guesses at the reason—that the bishop wished to avoid being asked to explain difficult passages to his listeners, or to spare a voice that tired easily—concern why a man would read silently in company, not whether such reading was possible. A single surprised witness, in any case, tells us first of all about the witness's own expectations. Whether those expectations were shared by everyone who could read is another question.
options: Silent reading may well have been rarer in antiquity than modern scholars tend to assume.
Augustine misunderstood the reasons why Ambrose chose to read in silence.
Silent reading was in fact widespread in the ancient world, as Augustine's account shows.
Augustine's account says less about ancient reading habits than is often assumed.
explain: The author's central claim is that 'the inference is weaker than it looks': the scene has long been cited as proof that silent reading was rare, but the circumstances and Augustine's own guesses suggest that it shows something narrower. The suggestion that silent reading may have been rarer than modern scholars assume runs against this argument, which weakens the evidence for rarity rather than strengthening it. Nor does the text claim that Augustine misunderstood Ambrose's reasons; his guesses are used as evidence of what puzzled him. Finally, the author does not argue that silent reading was widespread, since whether Augustine's expectations were shared by other readers is left as 'another question'.

prompt: According to the text, why may a document saved thirty years ago be impossible to read today?
passage: A letter left in a drawer for three hundred years can usually still be read by anyone who knows the language. A document saved on a computer thirty years ago may be beyond rescue even if the disk that holds it is in perfect condition. The bits survive; what disappears is everything needed to make sense of them—the program that created the file, the operating system that ran the program, the machine that ran the operating system. Each layer was built on the unspoken assumption that the one beneath it would always be there. Seen this way, preserving digital material has less in common with storing objects than with keeping a language in use. Putting files somewhere safe is only the beginning; someone must go on carrying them over into forms that the tools of the day can open, again and again, for as long as anyone wants them read. A digital archive, in other words, is less a place than an activity.
options: The data on the disk fades gradually, even when the disk itself is well kept.
Modern computers are designed to refuse files made on much older systems.
The programs and machines needed to open it may no longer exist.
No one may still remember what the document was originally for.
explain: The text says that 'the bits survive' and that what disappears is everything needed to make sense of them: 'the program that created the file, the operating system that ran the program, the machine that ran the operating system'. The idea that the data fades contradicts this, as well as the statement that the disk may be in perfect condition. Nothing is said about modern computers being designed to refuse old files; the problem is that the layers needed to read them have disappeared. And 'make sense of them' refers to these technical layers, not to people forgetting what a document was for.

prompt: What is the main point of the text?
passage:
Few medical messages are as easy to sell as the promise of early detection. Find a disease before it causes symptoms, the reasoning goes, and you can treat it while it is still small, simple and curable. It is hard to imagine anyone objecting, and in public campaigns hardly anyone does. Yet the figures most often quoted in support of screening are among the least reliable guides to whether it works.

Consider survival rates: the share of patients still alive, say, five years after diagnosis. Imagine a woman whose tumour, left to announce itself, would cause symptoms at the age of 64 and kill her at 68. Her survival after diagnosis would be four years. Now suppose that a screening test finds the same tumour at 58, and that the treatment she then receives makes no difference whatever. She still dies at 68, but she has now survived ten years after diagnosis and counts as a five-year survivor. The statistics have improved; her life has not been extended by a single day. All that has changed is the moment at which the clock was started.

A second distortion is less obvious and, in some ways, more troubling. Screening does not only find dangerous diseases earlier. It also finds abnormalities that would never have caused any harm: tumours that grow so slowly, or stop growing altogether, that the people carrying them would have died of something else without ever knowing they were there. Doctors call this overdiagnosis. Its victims are turned into patients and given treatment—surgery, radiotherapy, years of check-ups—from which they cannot benefit, because there was nothing to cure. And since no one can tell, in any individual case, which tumours belonged to this harmless group, every one of these people has reason to believe that the test saved their life.

The result is a paradox. The more overdiagnosis a programme causes, the more survivors it produces, the more grateful patients it has to speak on its behalf, and the more popular it becomes. A programme that did nothing but harm could, in principle, earn a reputation as one of medicine's great successes.

None of this means that screening is a mistake. For some diseases, large trials in which people were invited to screening or not, at random, have shown that fewer of those invited went on to die of the disease. That, rather than survival after diagnosis, is the figure that matters, because neither distortion can flatter it: starting the clock earlier does not, by itself, postpone a single death, and finding harmless tumours does not prevent one. The difficulty is that such trials take many years and very large numbers of people, and their results are rarely as dramatic as the stories told by survivors.

What follows is not that people should refuse to be screened, but that they deserve to be told what they are being offered. An invitation that mentions only the lives saved, and not the healthy people turned into patients, is not really asking for consent. It is asking for applause.

The figures and stories most often cited in support of screening say little about whether it saves lives.
Survival rates mislead chiefly because screening programmes start counting from the moment a tumour is found.
Screening ought to be offered only for diseases where large trials have shown that it prevents deaths.
explain: The author argues that survival figures can improve without anyone living longer, and that overdiagnosis creates grateful 'survivors' who were never in danger, so that even a programme that 'did nothing but harm' could look like a great success; the usual evidence therefore says little about whether screening saves lives. Starting the count at diagnosis is only one of the two distortions described, and the text does not single it out as the chief one; it even calls the second 'in some ways, more troubling'. A single distortion is in any case too narrow to be the main point. prompt: According to the reviewer, what is the novel's greatest strength?
passage:
Halfway through this first novel, its fifteen-year-old narrator watches her father wash the family car three times in a single afternoon. Nell does not know why he is doing it, and the novel does not stop to explain. It is the last week before the fish-processing plant where he has worked for twenty years closes its doors, and the reader grasps at once what she cannot: that a man who will soon have nowhere to go in the morning needs something to do with his hands. Nell notices only that the car has never been so clean.

Scenes like this are the novel's great strength. The closure of the plant, which employs half the town, is the largest event in the book, yet it happens almost entirely offstage. We glimpse it in telephone calls overheard through a bedroom floor, in a neighbour's sudden wish to sell her piano, in the disappearance of the smell that used to hang over the harbour. Nell is far more interested in a boy from the campsite than in redundancy payments, and through her the catastrophe arrives as a series of small puzzles. The effect is not to make the town's loss seem smaller but to make it sharper. We are always a step ahead of the narrator, and it is in the space between what she sees and what we understand that the novel does its work.

The prose is plain, almost to a fault. There are few metaphors and fewer adjectives, and some readers will find the opening chapters slow. They should persist. The plainness turns out to be a kind of tact: a more colourful style would have crowded out the reader, who is being asked, page after page, to supply what Nell leaves out.

The trouble begins in the final third. Having kept us at Nell's shoulder for two hundred pages, the author suddenly hands the story to the father, in a series of chapters that tell us what he was thinking on the afternoon of the car and on all the others. Nothing in them is false, and some of it is moving. But very little of it is news. We had understood him perfectly well through his daughter's incomprehension; to have him explained is to be told what we had already worked out for ourselves, and to lose the very gap that had given the book its force. First novels are usually faulted for putting too much in. This one's fault is subtler: its author seems not to trust that she has already put enough in.

The ending, in which a new employer arrives, the father finds work and nobody has to leave, is tidier than anything that precedes it. One can see the impulse—after so much quiet loss, the author wants to give her characters something—but tidiness is an odd reward for a book whose great virtue was its willingness to leave things unsaid. Still, the first two-thirds are as fine as anything I have read this year, and a writer who can sustain that kind of restraint for so long will surely learn to sustain it to the last page.
options: Its detailed account of how the closure of the plant affects the town's economy
Its use of the father's point of view to explain what his daughter cannot see
The way it allows readers to understand more than its young narrator does
The vivid and colourful language in which the town and its people are described
explain: The reviewer calls scenes like the one with the car 'the novel's great strength' and explains that 'we are always a step ahead of the narrator': the book does its work in the space between what Nell sees and what the reader understands. The closure is said to happen 'almost entirely offstage', so the book gives no detailed account of its economic effects. The chapters told from the father's point of view are what the reviewer criticises, not praises. And the prose is described as 'plain, almost to a fault', with few metaphors and fewer adjectives.

Walk through almost any city park and you will find them: narrow strips of bare earth cutting across the grass where the paved path takes a longer way round. Every spring, volunteers in parks and nature reserves across much of Europe spend their weekends pulling up plants that are judged not to belong. The work is often described in military language. Unwanted species are 'invaders' or 'aliens'; they 'colonise' riverbanks and 'conquer' woodland; the volunteers who uproot them are fighting a 'war'. The vocabulary is so familiar that it is easy to forget it is a choice, and one that carries an argument within it: that a species which arrived with human help is, for that reason alone, an enemy.

Some introduced species have certainly earned the hostility. When the brown tree snake reached the Pacific island of Guam, probably as a stowaway in military cargo shortly after the Second World War, it found an abundance of birds that had never had to deal with a climbing predator. Within a few decades most of the island's native forest birds had disappeared. Stories like this are the reason why biologists take introductions seriously, and they are not rare.

They are, however, unrepresentative. Of all the species that people carry to new places, deliberately or by accident, the great majority fail to survive in the wild at all. prompt: What does the reviewer appreciate about Coyle's portrayal of Robert FitzRoy?
passage:
Weather forecasts are among the few scientific predictions that most of us consult every day, and among the few we feel entitled to mock. Harriet Coyle's Tomorrow's Sky, a history of the forecast from the first newspaper predictions to the present, sets out to explain how something so routine came to be possible, and why it still so often feels unreliable.

The book is at its best in its first half, which follows a handful of people who tried to predict the weather before anyone was sure it could be done. Coyle is particularly good on Robert FitzRoy, the naval officer who began publishing daily forecasts in The Times in 1861 and was mocked in the press whenever they failed. She resists the temptation to make him a martyr to science. Her FitzRoy is stubborn and thin-skinned, as quick to blame his critics as his instruments, and all the more sympathetic for it. Equally memorable is her account of Lewis Fry Richardson, who during the First World War spent weeks working out by hand a forecast for a single six-hour period, using the kind of physical equations that computers now solve. His result was wildly wrong, and Coyle shows with real skill why the failure was more instructive than many successes: his method was sound, but the data and the arithmetic available to him were not up to it.

The trouble begins when the story reaches the age in which the method finally worked. The arrival of satellites and electronic computers, which turned a speculative craft into a reliable service, is covered in a single chapter, and a hurried one. A reader would learn more from a few pages of a decent textbook about how today's forecasts are actually made. It is hard not to suspect that Coyle simply finds the earlier period more congenial: it has more eccentrics in it, and fewer committees.

That preference also shapes the argument that runs through the book. Coyle's central claim is that the history of forecasting is a history of learning to be uncertain. Early forecasters offered confident statements and were ridiculed when these turned out wrong; their modern successors speak of a seventy per cent chance of rain, and in doing so tell us something more honest about what can be known. It is an attractive idea, and in places a genuinely illuminating one. But it is repeated so often, and applied to so many episodes, that it begins to look less like a conclusion than a lens fitted before the evidence was examined. Forecasters did not, after all, begin to express themselves in probabilities simply because they became more modest. They did so in large part because they acquired the means of calculating those probabilities, and those means are exactly what the hurried chapter leaves out.

Coyle writes clear and often elegant prose, though she is too fond of meteorological metaphor; by the time a disagreement between two committees had been described as 'a cold front moving through the department', this reader was longing for plainer language. Such lapses are minor. The larger problem is one of balance, and it is a pity, because the material she has chosen to dwell on is handled with real distinction.

Tomorrow's Sky is, in the end, a fine book about the past of forecasting and a thin one about its present. Readers who want to know why the forecast on their phone is so much better than it was a generation ago will have to look elsewhere. Those who want to know why anyone attempted it in the first place could hardly do better.
options: It shows how unfairly the press treated a pioneer of science.
It presents him as a flawed man rather than as a heroic victim.
It explains why his forecasts were better than his critics thought.
It shows that his stubbornness was the key to his later success.
explain: The reviewer praises Coyle for resisting 'the temptation to make him a martyr to science': her FitzRoy is 'stubborn and thin-skinned' and 'all the more sympathetic for it', so he appears as a man with faults rather than as a heroic victim. Saying that the book shows how unfairly the press treated him reverses this point, since portraying him as wronged by his critics is exactly the martyr's story Coyle avoids. The review does not say that his forecasts were better than his critics believed, and his stubbornness is presented as a flaw of character, not as the reason for any success.

prompt: What weakness does the reviewer find in Coyle's central claim?
passage:
Weather forecasts are among the few scientific predictions that most of us consult every day, and among the few we feel entitled to mock. Harriet Coyle's Tomorrow's Sky, a history of the forecast from the first newspaper predictions to the present, sets out to explain how something so routine came to be possible, and why it still so often feels unreliable.

The book is at its best in its first half, which follows a handful of people who tried to predict the weather before anyone was sure it could be done. Coyle is particularly good on Robert FitzRoy, the naval officer who began publishing daily forecasts in The Times in 1861 and was mocked in the press whenever they failed. She resists the temptation to make him a martyr to science. Her FitzRoy is stubborn and thin-skinned, as quick to blame his critics as his instruments, and all the more sympathetic for it. Equally memorable is her account of Lewis Fry Richardson, who during the First World War spent weeks working out by hand a forecast for a single six-hour period, using the kind of physical equations that computers now solve. His result was wildly wrong, and Coyle shows with real skill why the failure was more instructive than many successes: his method was sound, but the data and the arithmetic available to him were not up to it.

The trouble begins when the story reaches the age in which the method finally worked. The arrival of satellites and electronic computers, which turned a speculative craft into a reliable service, is covered in a single chapter, and a hurried one. A reader would learn more from a few pages of a decent textbook about how today's forecasts are actually made. It is hard not to suspect that Coyle simply finds the earlier period more congenial: it has more eccentrics in it, and fewer committees.

That preference also shapes the argument that runs through the book. Coyle's central claim is that the history of forecasting is a history of learning to be uncertain. Early forecasters offered confident statements and were ridiculed when these turned out wrong; their modern successors speak of a seventy per cent chance of rain, and in doing so tell us something more honest about what can be known. It is an attractive idea, and in places a genuinely illuminating one. But it is repeated so often, and applied to so many episodes, that it begins to look less like a conclusion than a lens fitted before the evidence was examined. Forecasters did not, after all, begin to express themselves in probabilities simply because they became more modest. They did so in large part because they acquired the means of calculating those probabilities, and those means are exactly what the hurried chapter leaves out.

Coyle writes clear and often elegant prose, though she is too fond of meteorological metaphor; by the time a disagreement between two committees had been described as 'a cold front moving through the department', this reader was longing for plainer language. Such lapses are minor. The larger problem is one of balance, and it is a pity, because the material she has chosen to dwell on is handled with real distinction.

Readers who want to know why the forecast on their phone is so much better than it was a generation ago will have to look elsewhere. Those who want to know why anyone attempted it in the first place could hardly do better.

prompt: What is the main point of the text?
passage:
Anyone who has spent a night on a hospital ward will remember the noise. Monitors beep when a patient's heart rate rises or falls, infusion pumps chime when a bag runs empty, and sensors sound when a clip slips off a finger. Each of these alarms exists for a good reason, and each was added by someone who wanted to make patients safer. Taken together, however, they may be doing the opposite.

The problem is not that alarms fail to go off, but that they go off far too often. Studies of intensive care units have repeatedly found that most alarms require no action at all: the patient has moved, a cable has come loose, or a reading has briefly crossed a limit and returned to normal of its own accord. Staff who hear hundreds of such signals in a shift learn, quite reasonably, that an alarm usually means nothing. They respond more slowly, silence devices without checking, or widen the limits until the machines fall quiet. Nurses call this alarm fatigue, and it has been linked to cases in which a genuine emergency went unnoticed because the signal announcing it sounded exactly like the hundred false ones that preceded it.

What makes the problem stubborn is that no one is responsible for it. A manufacturer who sets a monitor to sound at the slightest irregularity is protected if something goes wrong; a manufacturer who sets it to stay quiet is not. Every individual decision to add an alarm, or to make one more sensitive, is easy to defend. The total, which is what the nurse actually has to live with, is no one's decision at all.

Some hospitals have shown that the noise can be reduced without any loss of safety. Adjusting limits to the individual patient rather than relying on factory settings removes many false alarms. So does adding a delay of a few seconds, since a large share of alarms correct themselves almost at once. Sending alerts directly to the nurse responsible for a patient, rather than broadcasting them to the whole ward, means that fewer people hear signals that are not meant for them. None of these measures is technically demanding. What they require is a willingness to accept that an alarm which never sounds unnecessarily will occasionally stay silent when it should have sounded, and that this risk may be smaller than the one it replaces.
options: Hospital alarms are often poorly designed because manufacturers ignore nurses' needs.
Nurses have grown careless about responding to the alarms on their wards.
Alarms in intensive care should be replaced by more frequent checks by staff.
Alarms that are each meant to protect patients can together make care less safe.
explain: The first paragraph sets out the thesis: each alarm 'was added by someone who wanted to make patients safer', but 'taken together' they may be doing the opposite; the rest of the text explains how too many signals lead staff to miss real emergencies and how the number could be reduced. Manufacturers' settings are explained by their wish to be protected if something goes wrong, not by indifference to nurses, and they are only part of the problem. The author describes staff as learning 'quite reasonably' that an alarm usually means nothing, which does not amount to calling them careless. And the remedies proposed adjust the alarms rather than replace them with checks by staff.

prompt: According to the text, what weakness do some scholars see in the painted reconstructions?
passage:
The white marble statues of ancient Greece and Rome have long stood for a particular ideal of beauty: calm, pure and free of decoration. Yet many of them were never meant to be white. Traces of pigment survive on a great number of ancient sculptures, and with the help of ultraviolet light and chemical analysis researchers have been able to reconstruct patterned clothing, coloured eyes and painted skin. The ancients, it seems, painted their statues, and often brightly.

Reconstructions based on this evidence regularly provoke dismay. Visitors to exhibitions of painted copies have described them as garish, even vulgar, and some scholars have objected that the reconstructions rest on so little surviving paint that they are partly guesswork. That objection has some force: a fleck of blue on a fold of drapery does not reveal the exact shade, or how it was combined with other colours. But the discomfort seems to have older roots. The admiration for white marble took shape in the eighteenth century, when the paint had long since weathered away, and writers who knew the statues only in their faded state built a whole theory of classical taste largely on that absence. What looks like a reaction to bad reconstruction may often be loyalty to that theory.
options: Much of what they show cannot be read from the surviving traces of paint.
They use pigments that would not have been available in antiquity.
They may reproduce paint that was added long after the statues were made.
Their colours are brighter than modern visitors find tasteful.
explain: Some scholars object that the reconstructions 'rest on so little surviving paint that they are partly guesswork', and the author agrees that a fleck of blue does not reveal the exact shade or how it was combined with other colours; much of what the copies show must therefore be filled in. The text says nothing about anachronistic pigments or about paint added after antiquity. The complaint that the colours are garish comes from visitors, not from the scholars, and concerns taste rather than evidence.

prompt: What does the author mean by saying that crowd figures are 'easy to bend without anyone telling an outright lie'?
passage:
After almost every large demonstration, two numbers appear. The organisers announce one, the police another, and the gap between them is often so wide that it is tempting to assume both are invented. In fact, counting a crowd is not especially mysterious. The standard method, developed in the 1960s, is to divide the area the crowd occupies into sections, estimate how densely people are packed in a sample of them, and multiply. A loosely gathered crowd might have one person per square metre; in a tightly packed one, where people can barely move, there may be four or more.

The arithmetic is simple. The difficulty lies in the inputs, and especially in density, which varies enormously across a single crowd. The area just in front of a stage may be packed solid while the edges are thin, and an estimate that takes the dense centre as typical can easily double the true figure. Marches create a further problem, because people come and go. A count of everyone present at the moment of peak attendance will miss those who joined for an hour and left early, while adding up everyone who passes a given point risks counting the same people twice if the route loops back on itself.

None of this means that the figures are arbitrary, but it does mean that they are easy to bend without anyone telling an outright lie. Organisers have an obvious interest in large numbers and authorities sometimes in small ones, and each side can choose, honestly enough, the assumptions that suit it. Independent estimates based on aerial photographs tend to fall between the two, though not always in the middle.

The most useful question to ask about a crowd figure, then, is not whether it is true, but how it was produced. A number that comes with its method attached (the area measured, the densities assumed, the time of day) can be checked and argued with. A number without one can only be believed or disbelieved, and people tend to believe whichever figure flatters the cause they already support.
options: Organisers and the police often agree in private on figures other than those they publish.
Different but defensible assumptions can produce very different totals.
Small errors in counting tend to grow as figures are passed on to the press.
The figures are often rounded up in ways that are difficult to detect.
explain: The next sentence explains the remark: each side 'can choose, honestly enough, the assumptions that suit it'. Because density and attendance vary so much, reasonable choices of input can lead to very different totals without anyone inventing a number. Private agreements between organisers and the police are never mentioned. The text does not describe errors growing as figures are passed on, and rounding up is not discussed; the point concerns the assumptions behind the calculation.

prompt: Why, according to the text, did Ise once seem 'a puzzle, even a scandal' to many European conservationists?
passage:
At Ise, the most sacred buildings of Japan's most important Shinto shrine are taken down roughly every twenty years and rebuilt, in fresh cypress wood, on a neighbouring plot. The practice has continued, with some interruptions, for well over a thousand years. The buildings a visitor sees today are therefore only a few years old, and yet they are widely regarded as one of the oldest living traditions of Japanese architecture.

To many European conservationists, this once seemed a puzzle, even a scandal. Their own tradition held that what deserves protection is original material: the stones actually laid by medieval masons, the timbers actually cut in the year a church was built. Replacing such material, however faithfully, was thought to destroy precisely what made a building valuable. By that standard, Ise has nothing left to protect.

Yet the rebuilding preserves something that the European approach can lose. Each reconstruction requires carpenters who know the old techniques, and the twenty-year cycle ensures that the knowledge is passed on before those who hold it grow too old to work. A medieval church whose every original beam has been carefully preserved may stand intact while the skills needed to build it have long since vanished. Since the 1990s, international guidelines on heritage have recognised that authenticity can reside in form, use and tradition as well as in material. Ise did not change its practice to fit that view; the view, in part, was changed to make room for Ise.
options: The rebuilding destroyed buildings that had stood for over a thousand years.
The new buildings were not faithful copies of the ones they replaced.
They doubted that the tradition had really continued without interruption.
They located a building's value in the material it was originally made of.
explain: The European tradition held that 'what deserves protection is original material', and that replacing it 'however faithfully' destroys what makes a building valuable; buildings that are replaced every twenty years thus seemed to have 'nothing left to protect'. It is the practice of rebuilding, not the buildings, that is over a thousand years old; each building stands for only about twenty years. The text does not suggest that the new buildings are unfaithful copies, and the phrase 'however faithfully' shows that even faithful copies would not have satisfied the European view. The interruptions are mentioned by the author and are not presented as the source of the conservationists' objection.

prompt: What is the main point of the text?
passage:
Few environmental pledges photograph as well as a promise to plant trees. A politician with a spade, a row of saplings, a number with plenty of zeros: the image suggests a problem being solved by hand, one seedling at a time. Trees do draw carbon dioxide out of the air and store it in wood and soil, and forests do much else besides, from holding hillsides together to sheltering wildlife. It is easy to see why planting has become a favourite climate gesture of governments and companies alike.

The difficulty lies less in the trees than in the counting. A pledge is usually measured in saplings put into the ground, because that is the figure that can be announced on the day. But a sapling is not a forest. In dry years, or where nobody is paid to water and weed, a large share of young trees may die within a few seasons, and a campaign that reports what was planted rather than what survived can claim success for a hillside that is bare again a decade later. Even the trees that live take decades to store the carbon with which they are credited at the outset, while the emissions they are meant to make up for enter the atmosphere at once.

Where the trees go matters as much as how many there are. Planting on land that was forest until recently can restore much of what was lost. Planting on natural grassland or peat bog is another matter. Such landscapes may look empty to a visitor, but many hold large amounts of carbon below ground and support species found nowhere else; covering them with fast-growing conifers can release some of that carbon and drive out the very wildlife a project claims to help. In snowy regions, a dark canopy that replaces pale ground can even absorb more of the sun's heat, cancelling part of the cooling the trees provide.

None of this means that planting is pointless. It means that the number on the press release is a poor guide to the benefit. Several researchers have argued that the cheapest and most reliable way to gain a forest is often not to plant one at all but to let one return: to protect land from grazing or clearing and allow trees to seed themselves, as they will in many places if left alone. Such forests are less dramatic to launch and harder to photograph, since for the first few years there is little to show but scrub. They also tend to suit local conditions better, because the trees that arrive are the ones the land can support.

The deepest worry, however, concerns not the trees but what they may excuse. A company that promises to plant its way to 'net zero' is making a claim about the future in exchange for permission to go on emitting in the present. Forests can burn, be felled or die in a drought, and the carbon in them can return to the air far more quickly than it was stored. Planting is best seen as an addition to cutting emissions rather than a substitute for it—a useful thing to do with a spade, provided the spade is not also used to bury the question of what comes out of the chimney.
options: Tree planting has become popular mainly because it is so easy to present well to the public.
Letting forests return by themselves works better than planting trees in almost every case.
Tree-planting pledges tend to promise more for the climate than they can reliably deliver.
Planting trees does the climate more harm than good when it is done on the wrong kind of land.
explain: The author accepts that trees store carbon and that planting is not 'pointless', but argues that the figures announced say little about the real benefit: many saplings die, carbon is stored only slowly, planting in the wrong place can backfire, and promises to plant may excuse continued emissions. Pledges therefore tend to promise more than planting can reliably deliver. That planting is popular because it photographs well is said in the first paragraph, but only as the starting point for the argument. Letting forests return is said to be 'often' the cheapest and most reliable option, not better in almost every case. Planting on grassland or bog is one problem among several, and the author does not claim that it does more harm than good overall.

prompt: Why does the author begin with the example of the twenty research teams?
passage:
Imagine twenty research teams, working independently, all testing whether a certain food supplement improves memory. Suppose it does nothing at all. By the ordinary rules of statistics, which accept a one-in-twenty risk of mistaking chance for a real effect, one of the teams can be expected, on average, to find a 'significant' result anyway. That team writes up its study, and a journal, pleased with a clear and surprising finding, publishes it. The other nineteen, with nothing to report but a flat line, put their data in a drawer and move on. Anyone who later searches the literature will find a single study, and it will say that the supplement works.

This is the 'file-drawer problem', and it does not require anyone to cheat. Each decision along the way is understandable. Researchers have limited time and would rather spend it on work that might be published; editors want papers that others will cite; and a study reporting that something has no effect can seem, to all concerned, like a study in which nothing happened. Yet the sum of these sensible choices is a record that systematically overstates how often things work, and the distortion is invisible from inside, because the missing studies leave no trace.

Several remedies have been tried. Some journals now accept papers on the basis of the question and the methods, before any results exist, and promise to publish whatever the data turn out to show. In some fields, trials must be registered before they begin, so that a study which quietly disappears can at least be seen to be missing. Statisticians have devised ways of estimating, from the pattern of published results, how many unpublished ones there are likely to be, though such estimates rest on assumptions that are hard to check.

What these measures have in common is that they change not the honesty of researchers but the incentives around them. That is probably the right target. Appeals to publish negative results have been made for decades, with little effect, because they ask individuals to bear a cost for a benefit that is shared by everyone. A null result that is published is a small gift to the field: it saves others from repeating a dead end and corrects the impression left by luckier studies. The trouble is that, under the present system, the researcher who gives that gift is rarely the one who is thanked for it.
options: To show how easily researchers are tempted to report their data dishonestly.
To suggest that studies of food supplements are especially unreliable.
To argue that most of the findings published in science are probably false.
To show how a false impression can arise even if every study is honest.
explain: In the example no one does anything wrong: one team finds a 'significant' result by chance, the others leave their results unpublished, and the literature ends up saying that a useless supplement works. The author then stresses that the problem 'does not require anyone to cheat'. The example thus shows how a misleading picture can arise from honest studies, which rules out the reading that it is about dishonest reporting. The supplement is merely an illustration, and nothing suggests that such studies are especially unreliable. The text says that the record overstates how often things work, which is not the same as claiming that most published findings are false.

prompt: According to the text, why does the low cost of dimming the sun raise a new kind of problem?
passage:
Of all the proposals for dealing with a warming climate, few provoke as much unease as the idea of dimming the sun. The principle is simple enough. Large volcanic eruptions throw fine particles high into the atmosphere, where they reflect a little sunlight back into space, and for a year or two afterwards the world is measurably cooler. A deliberate programme might do the same by releasing particles from high-flying aircraft, and do it, by most estimates, at a cost that is small compared with that of the damage it might prevent.

That cheapness is part of the problem. Cutting emissions requires almost every country to act, and each is tempted to let the others go first. Dimming the sun would require no such cooperation: a single country, or even a wealthy consortium, could in principle attempt it alone. A technology cheap enough for one actor to use raises a question that climate politics has never had to face—not who will pay for action, but who will be allowed to take it, and on whose behalf.

Then there is what such a programme would leave untouched. Reflecting sunlight would offset some of the warming caused by greenhouse gases but would do nothing about the gases themselves. Carbon dioxide would go on accumulating, and the oceans would go on absorbing it and growing more acidic. The cooling, meanwhile, would last only as long as the particles were replenished, since they fall out of the atmosphere within a few years. Were a programme to be stopped abruptly—by war, say, or by a change of government—temperatures could rise towards the level they would have reached without it, and do so far faster than if they had climbed gradually. The world would have bought time on condition of never ceasing to pay for it.

Critics also fear the effect of the idea itself. If governments came to believe that warming could be switched off at will, the argument goes, the pressure to cut emissions would ease. Defenders reply that the same was once said of preparing for floods and droughts: that talk of adaptation would weaken the commitment to prevention. prompt: According to the text, why can taking on technical debt be a sensible choice?
passage:
Software engineers have borrowed a term from finance to describe a problem that their managers often fail to see. 'Technical debt' is what builds up when a program is written quickly rather than well: a shortcut taken to meet a deadline, a patch added instead of a redesign, a section of code that only its author understands. Like a loan, such a shortcut can be perfectly sensible. A company that ships a rough product in time to win customers may be better off than one that ships a polished product too late. The trouble is that the debt carries interest. Every later change to a tangled program takes a little longer and risks breaking something unexpected, and the cost grows with each new shortcut piled on top of the old ones.

The metaphor has been useful, not least because it gives engineers a language that managers understand. But it can also mislead. A financial debt has a known size and a schedule of payments; technical debt is usually discovered only when someone tries to change the code, and its size may be impossible to estimate in advance. Nor is it always the borrower who pays. Programs often outlive the teams that wrote them, so that the interest falls on people who never took the loan and may not know it exists. Some engineers have therefore suggested that a better comparison would be with pollution: a cost created in one place and quietly passed on to someone else.
options: Tidying up the code later usually costs less than people expect.
Programs built quickly are easier for managers to understand.
Being early can matter more to a business than being thorough.
Shortcuts are usually removed the next time the program is changed.
explain: The text says that 'a company that ships a rough product in time to win customers may be better off than one that ships a polished product too late', so speed can sometimes be worth more than quality. The idea that tidying up later costs less than expected contradicts the claims that the debt 'carries interest' and that its size may be impossible to estimate in advance. What managers understand is the financial metaphor, not programs that were built quickly. And the text describes new shortcuts being piled on top of old ones, not shortcuts being removed when the program is changed.

prompt: What does the author mean by saying that the sceptics 'turned out to be partly right and largely irrelevant'?
passage:
When a team of astronomers first invited members of the public to help sort images of galaxies by shape, many colleagues expected the results to be useless. The volunteers had no training beyond a short online tutorial, and it seemed obvious that their judgements would be less reliable than those of professionals. The sceptics turned out to be partly right and largely irrelevant. Any single volunteer did make more mistakes than an expert. But each image was shown to many volunteers, and the combined verdict of the crowd proved, for most purposes, as good as that of a specialist—and it could be produced for hundreds of thousands of images, a task no team of experts could have completed.

Projects of this kind have since multiplied, from transcribing old ships' weather logs to spotting animals in photographs taken by hidden cameras. Their value does not lie only in the labour they supply. Volunteers, being untrained, sometimes notice what experts have learned to ignore, and several unusual objects have come to light because someone simply asked about something odd in an image. Yet the model has limits. It works best when a task can be broken into many small judgements that are easy to compare with one another, and less well when a judgement requires long experience. It also depends on a supply of enthusiasm that cannot be taken for granted: a project that treats its volunteers merely as unpaid processors tends to lose them.

Volunteers made more mistakes than experts, but only when classifying unusual images.

prompt: According to the text, how can a sea wall create the need for more walls?
passage:
For centuries the usual answer to a rising sea has been to build a wall. Walls are visible, they protect the land behind them at once, and their benefits are easy to explain to the people whose homes they shelter. They also have a way of creating the need for more of themselves. Land behind a wall feels safe, so it is built on; the more valuable it becomes, the stronger the case for raising the wall again when the sea rises further. Meanwhile, the beach or marsh in front of the wall, unable to move inland as it naturally would, is gradually squeezed out of existence—and with it the natural buffer that once absorbed some of the force of the waves.

An alternative, sometimes called managed retreat, is to allow parts of the coast to flood and to move people and buildings away from the most exposed places in an orderly way. In some places, old sea walls have been deliberately breached so that farmland can turn back into salt marsh, which then helps to protect the land behind it. Engineers often describe such schemes as cheap and effective. Residents tend to describe them differently. To an engineer, a field returned to the sea is a sensible trade; to the family who farmed it, it is a loss that no calculation of averages will make good. The hardest part of retreat is rarely technical. It is deciding who must move, who will pay, and who has the right to decide.
options: It causes the sea along that stretch of coast to rise faster than before.
It weakens as the sea rises and must then be rebuilt in an even stronger form.
It encourages building on land that then becomes too valuable to give up.
It makes residents unwilling to accept any other kind of protection.
explain: Land behind a wall 'feels safe, so it is built on', and the more valuable it becomes, the stronger the case for raising the wall again when the sea rises further. Nothing suggests that a wall makes the sea rise faster; the sea is said to rise in any case. Nor does the text say that walls weaken over time; they are raised because the water gets higher, not because they wear out. And the text does not say that residents refuse other kinds of protection, only that the benefits of walls are easy to explain to them and that residents see managed retreat differently from engineers.

prompt: What is the main point of the text?
passage:
Before a state can tax its subjects, conscript their sons or vaccinate their children, it has to be able to find them. This sounds trivial today, when almost everyone has an official name, a registered address and a number that follows them from birth to death. For most of history it was nothing of the kind. In many villages a man might be known by one name to his neighbours, by another in church, and by a description – the miller's son, the one who lives by the bridge – to anyone else. Land was held under customs that the people who used it understood perfectly well and that no outsider could read: a field might belong to one family for ploughing, to the whole village for grazing after the harvest, and to a widow for gleaning the grain that had been left behind.

To an official sent from the capital, such arrangements were less unjust than illegible. They could not be written down in a ledger, compared from one district to the next or added up into a total. Much of what we call the growth of the modern state can be described as a long campaign to make society readable from above. Permanent surnames, which in some countries were imposed by officials rather than chosen by families, made it possible to keep track of individuals across generations. Surveyed maps turned tangled local customs into plots with a single owner and a clear boundary. Standard weights and measures replaced the bushel that varied from one market to the next.

It would be easy to tell this story as one of simple oppression, and some of its episodes deserve no kinder description. But legibility also made possible much that we now take for granted. A pension cannot be paid to someone the state cannot identify, and a vaccination campaign cannot reach children who do not appear in any register. The same records that allowed a government to find young men for its armies later allowed it to find old people who were owed support.

The more troubling lesson lies elsewhere. A simplified picture is useful precisely because it leaves things out, and officials who work with it every day can forget that anything has been left out. When the map is mistaken for the territory, reforms designed on paper can fail in practice – not because their designers were wicked, but because the knowledge that would have warned them existed only in the arrangements they had swept away. The village that shared its fields in complicated ways was often managing risk: no family was ruined by a single bad harvest on one plot. Divided into neat private holdings, the same land could look more rational and leave its owners more exposed.

None of this is an argument against registers or maps. It is an argument for remembering what they are: tools for seeing some things clearly by agreeing not to look at others.
options: Local ways of sharing land were usually fairer and safer than the private plots that officials put in their place.
Making society readable from above has real benefits, but the simplified view it needs can hide what matters.
The rise of the modern state is best understood as a campaign by officials to gain control over unwilling subjects.
Reforms planned on paper tend to fail because officials care more about their records than about the people they govern.
explain: The author describes how states made society 'readable from above', grants that this 'made possible much that we now take for granted', such as pensions and vaccination, and then warns that a simplified picture 'leaves things out', so that reforms can fail because the knowledge that would have warned officials had been swept away. The author explicitly declines to tell the story 'as one of simple oppression', so it is not best understood as a campaign against unwilling subjects. And the text blames failed reforms on officials forgetting what their picture leaves out, 'not because their designers were wicked', so it does not say that they cared more about records than about people.

prompt: According to the text, why must musicians' pay rise even though their productivity has hardly changed?
passage:
Why does a haircut cost so much more today than it did fifty years ago, when a television set costs so much less? The usual suspects – greedy hairdressers, rising rents, a lack of competition – explain little. A more convincing answer was offered by the economist William Baumol in the 1960s, and it begins, unexpectedly, with a string quartet.

A string quartet written in the eighteenth century needs four players and takes roughly as long to perform today as it did when it was composed. Over more than two centuries, the productivity of musicians, measured as performances per hour of work, has hardly changed. The productivity of workers who make cloth, cars or telephones, by contrast, has risen many times over. Yet musicians' pay has not stayed where it was. If it had, almost nobody would become a musician; people who might have played the viola would take better-paid work elsewhere instead. Wages in the stagnant sectors must therefore keep roughly in step with wages across the economy, even though productivity there does not. The result is that the cost of a concert, a haircut, a school lesson or a nursing shift rises steadily compared with the cost of goods whose production has become ever more efficient.

Baumol called this a 'disease', but he was careful to point out that it is a strange kind of illness. Services do not become more expensive because anything has gone wrong in them; they become relatively more expensive because something has gone right elsewhere. And because the economy as a whole is growing richer, society can in principle go on affording them. The danger is political rather than economic. When the budgets of schools and hospitals rise faster than inflation year after year, the increase looks like waste, and the natural response is to demand cuts or to search for inefficiencies that may not exist.

Not every service is stuck, of course. Banking and retail have been transformed by computers, and parts of medicine have become far more productive. prompt: According to the text, what did Columbus's critics actually object to?
passage:
Ask people what educated Europeans in the Middle Ages believed about the shape of the earth, and many will say that they thought it was flat, and that Columbus had to overcome fears that his ships would sail off its edge. The story is almost entirely false. Scholars of the period took the earth's roundness for granted; it was taught in the universities and assumed in the most widely used textbooks of astronomy. The objection that Columbus actually faced was quite different and, as it turned out, correct: his critics argued that the earth was much larger than he claimed, so that no ship could carry enough supplies to reach Asia by sailing west. He was saved only because a continent unknown to either side lay in the way.

How, then, did the myth take hold? Historians have traced much of it to the nineteenth century, when popular biographies portrayed Columbus as a lone man of reason facing down superstitious churchmen, and when writers eager to present science and religion as natural enemies found in the flat earth a convenient symbol of the darkness that science had dispelled. The tale suited them too well to be checked.

The irony is that a story told to celebrate critical thinking has survived so long because so few people have thought critically about it. A myth about the credulity of the past turns out to be a fine example of credulity in the present.
options: He could not show that there was any land to the west of Europe at all.
His ships risked being lost at the edge of the known world.
He had greatly underestimated the distance he would have to sail.
His estimate of the earth's size was larger than their own.
explain: The critics 'argued that the earth was much larger than he claimed', so that no ship could carry enough supplies to reach Asia by sailing west; in other words, Columbus had underestimated the distance. The objection was not about whether there was land to the west, since the critics took Asia to lie there; their point was that it was too far away. The fear of being lost at the edge of the world belongs to the false story that the author corrects. And it was the critics, not Columbus, who held the larger estimate of the earth's size.

prompt: How does the author regard Hardin's argument?
passage:
In 1968 the ecologist Garrett Hardin published an essay whose title has outlived most of its arguments: 'The Tragedy of the Commons'. Imagine, he wrote, a pasture open to all. Each herder gains the full benefit of adding one more animal, while the cost – a little less grass for everyone – is shared by all. Every herder therefore has a reason to add animals, and the pasture is grazed to ruin. The essay was widely read as showing that shared resources must either be divided into private property or placed under the control of the state.

The argument is elegant, and under the conditions it assumes – users who never talk to one another and face no rules – it is correct. The trouble is that real commons rarely look like that. The political scientist Elinor Ostrom spent decades studying communities that had managed shared forests, fisheries and irrigation systems for generations without either dividing them up or handing them to a government. What the successful ones typically had in common was not exceptional virtue but structure: clear limits on who could use the resource, rules made by the users themselves, ways of keeping an eye on one another, and penalties that started small and grew with repeated offences.

Ostrom did not claim that self-government always works; she documented failures as well. Her point was that the choice is not limited to two options, and that outsiders who impose one of them can destroy arrangements that were working better than either.
options: As flawed in its logic, since herders would soon see that overgrazing harmed them too
As valid on its own assumptions, which seldom describe how commons are really used
As an accurate account of most commons that overlooks the role of the state
As correct in its own time but made obsolete by modern forms of regulation
explain: The author calls the argument 'elegant' and says that under the conditions it assumes, users who never talk to one another and face no rules, 'it is correct', but adds that 'real commons rarely look like that'. The logic is therefore not said to be flawed. Far from describing most commons accurately, the argument fits few of them, and state control is one of the two solutions the essay was read as recommending, so the state is hardly overlooked. Nor is the argument said to have been made obsolete by modern regulation; the communities Ostrom studied had managed their resources 'for generations'.

prompt: According to the text, what were the original Luddites mainly protesting against?
passage:
The word 'Luddite' is now used for anyone who distrusts new technology, usually with a hint of mockery. The original Luddites, textile workers in parts of England who smashed machines in the 1810s, deserve a fairer hearing. They were not, for the most part, opposed to machinery as such; many had worked with machines all their lives. Their anger was directed at particular employers who used new equipment to replace skilled workers with cheaper, less trained labour, to cut wages and to sell shoddy cloth that undercut the trade. Breaking frames was a way of putting pressure on those employers at a time when workers had no legal right to organise and no vote with which to change the law.

Seen in this light, the Luddites' question was not whether new machines should be used, but who should decide how they were used and who should share in the gains. Economists like to point out that mechanisation eventually made the country far richer and created more jobs than it destroyed, and over the long run they are right. But 'eventually' was a long time. For many of the workers involved, the gains arrived a generation too late, and for their children rather than for them.

That distinction – between what is good for an economy over decades and what happens to particular people in the meantime – is easily lost in today's arguments about automation. Both those who promise that new technology will benefit everyone and those who fear that it will leave millions without work tend to speak as if the outcome were decided by the machines themselves. The Luddites knew better: the outcome was decided by those who owned the machines, and by the laws under which they were used.
options: The use of machinery in a trade that had always been done by hand
Laws that denied them a vote and the right to organise
The way some employers used machines to undermine skilled workers
The poor quality of the machines they were made to operate
explain: The text says that the Luddites were 'not, for the most part, opposed to machinery as such' and that their anger was directed at 'particular employers' who used new equipment to replace skilled workers with cheaper labour and to cut wages. Many of them 'had worked with machines all their lives', so they were not protesting against machinery entering a hand trade. The lack of a vote and of the right to organise explains why they broke frames to put pressure on employers, not what they were protesting against. And the poor quality mentioned in the text concerns the cloth that undercut the trade, not the machines.

prompt: Why does the author regard the repeated issuing of the English wage laws as significant?

prompt: What 'awkward incentive' does the author point out?

prompt: What does the author conclude about microcredit?

The loans were repaid at remarkable rates, which seemed to prove that the poor were creditworthy after all. When economists finally tested the idea properly, by comparing similar areas that did and did not gain access to such loans, the results were sobering. Some borrowers did expand their businesses, but on average household incomes rose little, if at all. Yet the same studies found that borrowers valued the loans and used them, among other things, to cope with emergencies and to buy goods they would otherwise have had to save for slowly. The text does not say that it has done little good; borrowers 'valued the loans', and buying goods they would otherwise have had to save for is presented as one of the benefits. Nor does it say that most borrowers' incomes rose; on average they rose 'little, if at all'. And the repayment rates only 'seemed to prove' that the poor were creditworthy; the later studies showed that the loans did not, on average, lift borrowers out of poverty.

prompt: According to the text, how can compulsory voting affect the way parties campaign?
passage: Australia is one of a small number of democracies in which voting is compulsory: citizens who fail to vote without a valid reason can be fined, though the fine is small. Turnout at national elections is usually around ninety per cent. Defenders of the system tend to point to the legitimacy that comes from near-universal participation. A less obvious effect concerns how campaigns are fought. Where voting is voluntary, much of a party's effort goes into making sure that its own supporters actually turn up, and a message that excites the faithful, even if it repels everyone else, can be a winning strategy. Where almost everyone votes anyway, there is little to gain from rousing one's own side, and parties must instead win over voters with no strong attachment to either side. Critics reply that compulsion also brings to the polls people who know little and care less, and whose choice may be decided by something as trivial as the order of names on the ballot paper.

It encourages them to excite their own supporters, since every single vote must be won.
It allows them to spend less on campaigns, since high turnout is already assured.
It leads them to aim their messages at voters who know little about politics.
explain: The text says that where almost everyone votes anyway, 'there is little to gain from rousing one's own side', so parties must 'win over voters with no strong attachment to either side'. Exciting the faithful is described as a strategy that can work where voting is voluntary, which is the opposite case. Nothing is said about parties spending less. And voters who 'know little and care less' appear in the critics' objection about who is brought to the polls, not in the description of how parties campaign.

prompt: What is the main point of the text?
passage: A census looks like the most neutral of government activities: officials simply count who is there. But before anyone can be counted, someone must decide what the categories are, and that decision is rarely neutral. A question about religion, language or ancestry has to offer a list of answers, and the list tells people which identities the state recognises. Groups that appear on the form gain a number, and with it a claim on attention, funding and political representation; groups that do not appear are folded into 'other'. Not surprisingly, the wording of such questions is often fought over long before the census takes place. And once a category has been used for a few decades, it tends to harden: people come to describe themselves in its terms, organisations form around it, and changing it becomes politically difficult even when it no longer fits the way people live.
options: Governments often design censuses so as to reduce the size of unpopular groups.
The way a census sorts people can shape the groups it seems merely to count.
Census categories should be revised often so that they keep up with society.
Groups that are left off a census form tend to disappear within a few decades.
explain: The author argues that deciding the categories 'is rarely neutral': appearing on the form brings a claim on funding and representation, and a category used for decades 'tends to harden' as people describe themselves in its terms and organisations form around it. The census thus helps to shape the groups it appears simply to count. The text does not accuse governments of deliberately shrinking unpopular groups; it says only that groups not listed are folded into the category 'other'. It does not recommend frequent revision either, but notes that change becomes 'politically difficult'. And nothing is said about unlisted groups disappearing; the hardening over decades concerns categories that are used.

prompt: According to the political explanation in the text, why can oil wealth lead to worse government?
passage: Countries that discover large deposits of oil or minerals might be expected to prosper, yet many have grown more slowly, and been governed worse, than neighbours with no such luck. Economists call this the 'resource curse', and several explanations have been offered. One looks at the economy: a flood of export earnings can push up the value of the currency and make farming and manufacturing uncompetitive. Another looks at politics, and turns a familiar slogan on its head. A government that lives on taxes has to keep taxpayers at least partly content, and taxpayers who are asked for money tend to ask, in return, how it is spent. A government that lives on oil revenue needs its citizens far less. It can buy support, pay for a loyal army and ignore demands for accounts, because the money does not come from the people making the demands. The curse, on this view, lies not in the oil itself but in the independence from citizens that it buys.
options: Export earnings strengthen the currency so much that other industries decline.
Oil revenue allows rulers to raise taxes without fear of protest from citizens.
Governments spend their oil money on the army instead of on farming and industry.
Rulers who are not financed by taxes have less reason to answer to citizens.
explain: The political explanation is that a government living on taxes must keep taxpayers 'at least partly content' and answer their questions about spending, whereas one living on oil revenue 'needs its citizens far less' and can 'ignore demands for accounts'. The stronger currency belongs to the economic explanation, not the political one. The text does not say that oil allows rulers to raise taxes; the point is that they do not need taxes at all. And paying for a loyal army is mentioned as one way of staying in power, not as spending taken away from farming and industry, whose decline is part of the economic explanation.

prompt: What does the author mean by the final sentence of the text?
passage: A bank does not keep its depositors' money in a vault. It lends most of it out, keeping only a fraction on hand, on the reasonable assumption that depositors will not all want their money back at once. The arrangement is stable as long as everyone believes that it is. If depositors start to fear that the bank might fail, each of them has a good reason to withdraw before the others do, and the rush to withdraw can bring down even a bank whose loans are perfectly sound. The fear, in other words, can make itself come true. This is why government guarantees of deposits are so effective. If savers know that their money is safe whatever happens to the bank, they have no reason to join a run, and so runs do not start. A guarantee of this kind does its most important work on the days when nobody needs to claim it.

Such a guarantee protects savers mainly on the days when a bank has failed.

explain: The text explains that a guarantee is effective because savers who know their money is safe 'have no reason to join a run, and so runs do not start'; its most important work is preventing the fear that would otherwise make depositors withdraw. The text says nothing about what the guarantee costs, and it stresses that even a sound bank can be brought down by a run. The guarantee's main value lies on ordinary days, not on the days when a bank has failed. And it works precisely because savers know about it, since the text says 'if savers know that their money is safe'.

prompt: What is the main point of the text?

Within a few years, international conferences were agreeing on a standard format for the passport, including a photograph of its holder, and a document that had been an exceptional measure became an ordinary part of travel. Few people today would describe the passport as a wartime emergency measure, which is perhaps the clearest sign of how completely it has been absorbed into normal life.

Travel in Europe was freer before 1914 than it has ever been since then.

explain: The text describes how wartime controls 'stayed' after the fighting ended and how a document that had been 'an exceptional measure became an ordinary part of travel', so that today few people see the passport as an emergency measure at all. Spies and deserters are only part of the governments' worries, which also included 'who was leaving and entering their territory', and the text's point concerns what happened to the controls afterwards, not why they were introduced. The text compares travel only before and after 1914 and makes no claim about every later period.
