The diagnosis may be too kind to the decision-makers, or not kind enough. For the minister who launched the project, abandoning it means admitting a mistake in public, and the admission will be quoted at every election that follows. Continuing, by contrast, postpones the reckoning, perhaps until someone else holds the office. Seen from the minister's chair, carrying on may not be an error of reasoning at all. It may be a perfectly sensible choice – for the minister. The cost of that good sense is borne by the taxpayer.
options: It blames ministers for failures that were usually caused by their predecessors.
It ignores the fact that some projects that seem to be failing succeed in the end.
It assumes that ministers know less about their projects than commentators do.
It calls irrational a choice that may suit the minister but cost the public.

The text does not blame failures on predecessors; it is the minister who launched the project who would have to admit the mistake, and only the reckoning may pass to someone else. options: The prospect of emigrating may leave a country with more skilled people.
Emigration benefits a poor country as long as the emigrants send money back home.
Small countries suffer less from emigration, since fewer of their people leave.
The cost of educating emigrants is usually repaid when they return with savings.

prompt: According to the text, why may signature counts give a misleading picture of literacy in the past?
passage: Historians who want to know how many people could read in, say, the seventeenth century face an obvious problem: reading leaves no trace. What does leave a trace is writing, and in particular the signature. Marriage registers and legal documents show who signed their name and who made a mark instead, and counts of signatures have long served as the standard measure of literacy in the past. The method has the great virtue of being consistent across places and centuries. Its weakness lies in the way children were taught. Reading was usually taught first, and writing, if at all, a year or two later, by which time many children from poorer families had left school to work. A person who made a mark in the register might therefore have been able to read quite well. Signature counts may thus measure one skill accurately while understating another that was more widely shared.
options: Some people who were able to write chose to make a mark instead of signing.
Registers were kept more carefully in some places than they were in others.
Many people who never learnt to write may still have been able to read.
People could learn to sign their names without being able to read at all.
explain: The text explains that reading was usually taught first and writing 'a year or two later', by which time many poorer children had left school, so that a person who made a mark 'might therefore have been able to read quite well'. Nothing is said about people who could write choosing not to sign. The text praises the method for 'being consistent across places and centuries', so it does not point to differences in how registers were kept. And the error the text describes runs the other way: signature counts understate reading ability, rather than counting people who could sign but not read.

prompt: Which of the following would be the most suitable title for the text?
passage:
Ask people where they were when they heard some piece of shocking public news, and many will answer at once and in detail: the room, the person who told them, what they were holding at the time. Psychologists call such recollections 'flashbulb memories', a name that captures how they feel from the inside. They seem to have been recorded in an instant and preserved ever since, complete and unfaded, like a photograph taken by the glare of a flash.

The name, it turns out, flatters them. In a well-known kind of study, researchers ask people to write down how they learned of a dramatic event within a day or two of it happening, and then ask the same people again a few years later. The two accounts often differ, and not only in minor details. Someone who first wrote that she heard the news from a friend in a corridor may later describe, with complete conviction, watching it on television at home. When some participants were shown their own earlier accounts, they did not suddenly remember; a few insisted that the later version must be the right one, although the handwriting was plainly their own.

What sets these memories apart, then, is not their accuracy. Studies that have compared them with memories of ordinary events from the same days have found that both fade and change at a broadly similar rate. The difference lies elsewhere: people remain far more confident about the dramatic memory, and they recall it more vividly. The flashbulb, in other words, lights up our certainty more than it lights up the past.

Why should this be? One likely reason is that such memories are rehearsed. A shocking event is discussed for weeks, replayed in the media and retold at dinner tables, and each retelling is an opportunity for the story to be smoothed, borrowed from or quietly improved. By the time a memory has been told a hundred times, what we recall may be less the original experience than our most recent version of it. Another reason is that we need a place in the story. A public catastrophe is shared by millions; the memory of where we stood when we heard of it is what makes it ours.

None of this means that the memories are worthless, or that the people who hold them are deceiving anyone. They are telling the truth as it now exists for them. But it does suggest a caution that reaches well beyond psychology laboratories. Courts, historians and families all tend to treat a vivid, confident and detailed memory as more trustworthy than a hesitant one. The evidence of flashbulb memories suggests that vividness and confidence are at best weak signs of accuracy—and that the memories we would least think of doubting may be among those most in need of checking.
options: The day the news arrived: how shock sharpens memory
Vivid, confident and often wrong
Retelling as a cure for forgetting
Why witnesses to public disasters cannot be trusted
explain: The text argues that memories of shocking public news feel exceptionally clear and certain, but that they change over time as much as ordinary memories do, so that vividness and confidence are 'at best weak signs of accuracy'; a title stressing that such memories are vivid and confident yet often wrong captures this. The idea that shock sharpens memory is the impression the author sets out to correct. Retelling is presented as a likely reason why the memories change, not as a cure for forgetting. And the author does not say that witnesses cannot be trusted; the people who hold such memories are 'telling the truth as it now exists for them', and the advice is only that vivid memories may need checking.

prompt: What is the reviewer's main objection to the exhibition?
passage:
There is a familiar story about late style, and the curators of this exhibition clearly know it by heart. An artist grows old, loses patience with polish and convention, and in the final years produces work that is rougher, freer and more personal than anything before—work that the public of the day mistook for decline and that later generations recognised as the summit. The story has been told of composers, poets and painters alike, and it is now being told, on the walls of four large rooms, about Hendrika Maes, who painted the same stretch of coastline for more than fifty years and died, almost unknown outside her own country, in her late eighties.

The first room is the best argument for going. It hangs a dozen of Maes's early harbour scenes, careful, competent and slightly airless, alongside the sketchbooks she filled at the same time. The sketches are anything but airless. Boats are set down in three strokes, a squall in a smudge of the thumb. Seen together, the two suggest an artist who could already do in private what she would not yet risk in public.

That room, however, sits awkwardly with the argument the rest of the exhibition makes. The final two rooms, devoted to the paintings of her last decade, are presented as a breakthrough: wall texts speak of 'liberation' and of a painter 'finally free to see'. The canvases are certainly bold—sea and sky reduced to a few bands of colour, the horizon sometimes tilted, sometimes gone altogether—and several are very beautiful. But anyone who has just left the sketchbooks will recognise the freedom. It was there fifty years earlier. What changed in old age was not what Maes could see, but what she was willing to show.

That may seem a quibble, yet it matters. The story of late style flatters us, because it lets us believe that age and approaching death bring a kind of wisdom that can be read off the brushwork. It also lets curators skip over the decades in the middle, which here are represented by a single, crowded room. Those were the years in which Maes painted portraits for money, taught in a provincial school and exhibited rarely. They are less romantic than either the careful beginning or the blazing end, and the exhibition treats them as an interval to be walked through quickly. It is precisely there, I suspect, that the answer to the exhibition's real question lies: not how an old woman found her freedom, but why a young one waited so long to use it.

None of this should keep anyone away. The late canvases deserve to be seen at the scale for which they were made, and the sketchbooks alone are worth the ticket. Just be prepared to look past the wall texts. The exhibition has more to tell than the story it has chosen to tell.
options: It treats her late boldness as newly won, though the first room shows she had it decades earlier.
It gives too much space to careful early paintings that do not show Maes at her best and most original.
It hangs the late canvases in rooms that are too small for the large scale at which they were painted.
It overpraises the late paintings, which are in fact less accomplished than the work of her youth.
explain: The reviewer's objection is to the story the exhibition tells: the late rooms present Maes's bold style as a 'breakthrough' and a 'liberation', yet the sketchbooks in the first room show that the same freedom 'was there fifty years earlier'. The reviewer calls the first room 'the best argument for going', so there is no complaint that the early work takes up too much space. The remark about scale is a reason to visit, not a complaint: the late canvases 'deserve to be seen at the scale for which they were made'. And the reviewer finds several late paintings 'very beautiful', without ranking them below the early work.

prompt: What is the writer's main objection to the columnist's argument?
passage:
Sir,

Your columnist's lament for the word 'decimate' (Weekend, 14 March) was entertaining, but I fear it rests on a mistake that is older than the word itself. He objects that people now use 'decimate' to mean 'destroy almost entirely', when it 'really' means to kill one in every ten, as the Roman army is said to have done to punish mutinous legions. By his reasoning, a word means whatever it meant when it entered the language, and every later development is a kind of corruption.

I teach Latin, so I have some sympathy with anyone who enjoys knowing where words come from. But the history of a word is evidence of where it has been, not a ruling on where it may go. 'Nice' once meant foolish; nobody now thinks that a nice afternoon was a stupid one. If your columnist applied his principle consistently, he would have to object to half the words in his own article, starting, I suspect, with several that he has never stopped to look up.

Nor is it obvious that the old sense is the more useful one. The Roman practice, whatever its frequency, ended long ago, and a word that could only describe it would have very little to do. The modern sense, by contrast, fills a real gap: we have many words for destroying things completely, and rather fewer for damaging them so badly that what remains is barely recognisable.

None of this means that anything goes. Words can be misused, and a writer who uses 'decimate' to mean 'slightly reduce' deserves the red pen. But the test is whether the meaning is shared and clear, not whether it would have satisfied a centurion.

Yours faithfully,
Ruth Okafor, Leeds
options: It treats a word's first sense as the standard for judging all later uses.
It relies on a mistaken account of what the Roman army actually did to its soldiers.
It overlooks the fact that 'decimate' is now often used to mean 'slightly reduce'.
It treats Latin as a more important source of English words than any other language.
explain: The writer's complaint is that the columnist treats the meaning a word had when it entered the language as its true meaning and every later development as 'a kind of corruption'; she replies that 'the history of a word is evidence of where it has been, not a ruling on where it may go'. She does not dispute what the Roman army did, and even leaves its frequency open ('whatever its frequency'). Using 'decimate' to mean 'slightly reduce' is something she herself condemns, not a fact the columnist overlooked. And nothing in the letter suggests that the columnist rates Latin above other sources of English; it is the writer who teaches Latin.

prompt: What is the author's view of the complaint about 'literally'?
passage:
Few words provoke as much irritation among careful speakers as 'literally' used to mean its opposite. 'I literally died laughing,' says someone who plainly did not, and a certain kind of listener winces. The objection seems unanswerable: a word whose job is to mark that something is not a figure of speech is being used to decorate a figure of speech, and if it can mean both 'actually' and 'not actually', it would seem to mean nothing at all.

Yet the complaint has a weaker history than its confidence suggests. The intensifying use is not a recent invention of careless teenagers; it can be found in the work of respected novelists more than a century old. More importantly, it follows a path that many other words have taken before it. 'Very' comes from an old French word meaning 'true', and once meant something close to 'truly'; 'really' and 'truly' themselves are now used mostly to add emphasis, not to vouch for accuracy. Speakers seem to have a steady appetite for words that insist on their own sincerity, and the more such a word is used for emphasis, the less it insists. Each wears out and is replaced, and the replacement wears out in turn.

Nor, in practice, does the double meaning cause much confusion. Listeners rarely mistake 'I literally died laughing' for a report of a death, any more than they take 'I'm starving' as a medical claim. Context does the work, as it does for the many words that carry two meanings. What the intensifier does destroy is the usefulness of 'literally' as a precise tool in the rare cases where one needs it: the speaker who wants to say that the floor literally collapsed, not that the evening went badly, may now have to add 'and I mean that literally'. That is a real cost, but it is a cost paid by a few careful writers, not a collapse of meaning, and it is one that the language has paid many times before.
options: It turns a minor loss of precision into a supposed collapse of meaning.
It is fully justified, because the word can no longer mean anything at all.
It is mistaken, because the new use of the word costs the language nothing.
It is fair in substance, but it wrongly blames young people for the change.
explain: The author grants that the intensifying use has 'a real cost', since 'literally' becomes less useful in the rare cases where its strict sense is needed, but insists that this is 'not a collapse of meaning'; the complaint thus inflates a small loss. The view that the word now means nothing is the complaint itself, which the author argues against by showing that context prevents confusion. Saying that the change costs nothing goes too far, since the author admits a real cost. And the author does not accept the complaint in substance; the remark about teenagers is only one of several points made against it.

prompt: According to the text, why do passengers usually stay silent?
passage:
On a crowded morning train, the rule seems to be silence. Passengers sit inches apart, eyes on their phones or the window, and hardly anyone speaks. Most of us explain our own reserve in terms of other people: they would rather be left alone, we assume, and we would not want to impose.

Researchers who have tested that assumption have found it largely mistaken. In experiments of this kind, commuters were asked either to talk to a stranger, to keep to themselves, or to travel as they normally would. Before the journey, most predicted that a conversation would be the least pleasant option. Afterwards, those who had talked reported the most pleasant journeys, and very few had been rebuffed. The strangers, it seemed, were just as willing to talk; they were simply waiting, like everyone else, for someone else to begin.

What keeps the silence in place, then, is not a shared preference but a shared misjudgement. Each passenger underestimates how interested the others would be, and because nobody tests the belief, nobody discovers that it is wrong. Silence confirms itself: the quiet carriage looks like proof that people want quiet.

It would be easy to turn this into a campaign, and some have tried, with badges inviting conversation and posters urging people to say hello. The findings support a more modest conclusion. Some people on some journeys do want to be left alone, and a well-meaning stranger can be a burden. The point is not that we should all talk more, but that we are poor judges of when talking would be welcome, and that our errors tend to run in one direction.
options: Most of them would genuinely prefer to spend the journey alone with their thoughts.
They have learned from experience that strangers seldom welcome being spoken to.
Each of them wrongly expects that the others would not want to be spoken to.
They underestimate how pleasant a journey in silence can turn out to be.
explain: The text describes 'a shared misjudgement': each passenger underestimates how interested the others would be in talking, and since no one tests the belief, no one discovers that it is wrong. The text rejects the idea that the silence reflects a genuine preference ('not a shared preference'). Experience does not teach people that strangers are unwilling, since very few of those who talked were rebuffed; the belief survives precisely because it is not tested. And it is a conversation, not a silent journey, whose pleasantness people underestimate.

prompt: According to the critics described in the text, why could the performances not be truly 'authentic'?

For most of the twentieth century, a performance of Bach or Handel sounded much like a performance of Brahms: large orchestras, modern instruments, slow tempos and a generous sheen of vibrato. Then a movement of scholars and musicians set out to rescue the older music from these habits. prompt: According to the text, how do recent researchers see the link between nostalgia and low mood?

prompt: How does the author respond to the claim that proverbs are worthless?
